utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We understand counsel wishes to raise a matter. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, good afternoon. I just wanted to raise a question. You allowed me to spend this morning in a different case by moving this trial to this afternoon but you said that Wednesday was not possible, at least back then, but that you would do your best. There was information to indicate that the Seselj trial was to be held in this courtroom tomorrow afternoon. That trial has been cancelled, so I just wanted to see whether there was still an option for us to perhaps try this case in the afternoon tomorrow, since again tomorrow morning I will need to be in a different courtroom for the Blagojevic/Jokic case. I don't expect that I will be able to finish my cross-examination of this witness within a single session, assuming that Mr. Lukic will take up an entire session, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, our understanding is that Mr. Lukic will probably take the first session with the witness. Because of our shortened hours, it will be a slightly shortened session and that you were to have the second, with the possibility that you might creep into the third, but that was all, so that tomorrow, it would be Mr. Vasic who was here in the morning anyway, your role, active role would have finished, so you just would need to be sure that Mr. Vasic was alert to matters of interest to you. It's not that you would have any further role to play with this witness. But we will certainly look at the possibilities. There are a number of other commitments that people have taken up on the basis that we would be sitting in the morning. We will see. Can we have the witness, please. I would expect that we would finish the first session at 2.25, and the second session at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Lukic has some questions for you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, though I have copies of the expert report, we have three copies for the Chamber, a copy for each of the Defence teams, and a copy for the OTP. Your Honours, as you see, we compiled a special binder for your benefit containing the expert report of Mr. Vuga as well as 65 ter Defence documents which are mentioned in the report and which we will, in due course, be tendering into evidence. I think the most meaningful way to tender these documents is once Mr. Vuga has been heard, much like the procedure applying in the case of Mr. Theunens. That's one thing. The other thing that I wish to address orally, you might remember there was a written motion by the OTP requesting to cross-examine Mr. Vuga live and they opposed the idea for Mr. Vuga's annex regarding the historical context, historical framework in which the security service evolved in the Yugoslav army being admitted into evidence because it was, they submitted, irrelevant, and Mr. Vuga was not competent for that particular issue. That's at least based on my recollection. So my proposal now is to have his expert report admitted first with the annexes and to perhaps have a ruling on that particular annex at the end. The Defence will not be adamant about this annex being admitted, not necessarily, but we do believe some elements to be quite relevant for the substance of the report itself. We believe that the most helpful way to go about this would be to have a ruling at the end of Mr. Vuga's appearance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With that in mind, we can delay any decision until then, Mr. Lukic. But carry on, making use of the whole document including the annex if you need to. If it's ruled inadmissible, we'll just have to ignore certain parts of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, my first question, can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. My name is Petar Vuga, a retired colonel. I spent about 30 years working in the security organs, and I was called to testify before this Court as a security expert. I gladly responded to this invitation in the firm belief that my evidence might prove useful to the work of this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, are you the author of this expert report in front of you, the Defence expert report on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I am the author of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just two questions regarding your career. Generally speaking, the intention of our team in our examination-in-chief is to not go through everything that we have in the actual report but rather to focus on certain elements or certain aspects of your expert report which we believe to be particularly relevant or particularly typical of the general tenor of your expert report. A general question about your career. Over the course of your entire career, Mr. Vuga, were you involved on any sort of work on draft laws concerning security in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: When changes were made in the security organs, when new laws were to be drafted and literature was to be produced to train the personnel, I'd already had over 20 years of experience working in the security organs. It is for this reason that the leaders in the security sector called upon my contribution. Among other things, in 1983, I was involved, alongside with another three JNA officers, in investigating and carrying out a project entitled the situation and problems in terms of guiding security organs and measures for improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a footnote, you referred to the results of this particular piece of research. There's one thing in particular that I want to know about. Were you personally involved in the preparation, drafting and evaluation of a document that we here refer to as Exhibit 107, the rules of service for the security organ, the one that applied back in 1991? That set of rules is the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Following the research that I have referred to, the results of that particular work were used to produce the new set of rules. I was involved in analysing these results and defining a platform based on which the rules governing the work of the security organs were produced, and in 1991 this was the relevant document used for their work and the relevant set of rules that applied. I was also involved in drafting the proposed rules governing the work of security organs. It was later revised, this set of rules, and this new revised edition is the copy that we have in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that these new rules of the security organs, the rules that were evaluated and analysed in your report -- so is that document also a result of your involvement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, were you involved in drafting all the other documents, sublaws, instructions, and other documents that were used along with these rules for the security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I was involved in drafting all the operative rules and their application. I won't name all of them, but one of the most important ones was the instructions and -- for the methods of work of security organs and that was the one that I was the most involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That document is another exhibit in this trial. I will now move on to your career. I think what we have just gone through was of particular relevance towards proving your competence for the subjects that we are discussing here. The first page of your report tells us about what your report really is. I would like to read that out for the benefit of the public. All of us in the courtroom have this document in front of us. You wrote that the report contains: "The overview of the function of the security organs of the armed forces of the SFRY and the actions of the security organs and military police of the Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South on fulfilling all work and tasks they had within the provided territory, authority, and responsibility in Operation Vukovar in November 1991 with particular accent on Major now retired Colonel Veselin Sljivancanin while he was on the position of the chief of the security organ in the period of the indictment." In the briefest possible terms, this is what your report focuses on. We might say that. My question is: In paragraph 4 where you say that you would like to stress out that "I have primarily dealt with the security aspects of the acts within my report while I make notion of other aspects only as part of the general analysis," can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what it is that we are meant to focus on while studying your report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The distribution of the tasks of the security organ in any military organisation is quite large scale 6. It's intertwined with other types of activity, and it was very difficult to judge because it was very close to other activities. From the security aspect, it was difficult for them to be distinct from any other activity so that they might be identified so that whenever something happened, it might be possible to ascertain what really occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please. Purely in terms of methodology, how exactly did you produce this report? What was the method you used when you tackled the subject that your expert report addresses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The goal is defined on page 1 of this report. All the steps were envisaged that were necessary to achieve this goal. One needed to cover all the facts in relation to the function of the security organ. One needed to analyse these facts, make a comparative analysis in the light of the regulations under which the security organs were supposed to work. One needed to establish whether there was any distinction or any consistency with what really was the function that was carried out in the territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the sources that you used while you analysed this subject?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The principal sources that I used were the documents, the regulations that were to be followed in the territory and at the time that are the subject of my report. Secondly, I had statements available as well as combat documents. I studied everything else that was published about the function of the security sector and the events that significantly determined the function of security and its evolution as a very significant function. There are important elements that depend on what exactly happened between the two warring parties at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little clarification for the Chamber. In keeping with the instructions that the Chamber provided and the method that the Chamber applied when dealing with Mr. Pringle, Mr. Vuga invoked certain statements in the footnotes of his report. He was at one point shown the transcripts, too, and we developed a new system with footnotes containing sections of the transcript that are relevant for his report, whereas, on the other hand, we also dropped some of the transcript material previously used that did not prove to be as relevant. We did inform the OTP at the time. We had been in touch for that whole weekend and there was a motion with this final version of the expert report as a corrigendum with all the footnotes and the relevant sources specifically mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the regulations. Just a couple of questions related to this issue. The first question pertains to the scope of the activities of the security organs in the armed forces. We are now talking about page 9 in B/C/S and page 9 in the English version. Mr. Vuga, in simple terms, because we are all lawyers, can you please explain to us what is the scope of the activities of the security organs and why is this relevant for us in order to make it possible for us to understand their function and what Mr. Sljivancanin himself did? I think these are Article 1 through 5 of the rules of the service of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes. These are the articles that we're talking about. But let me make a general remark to preface all of this discussion, because this will make it possible for us to see the tasks in a much clearer light than we would be able to if we only had this text to guide us. The first thing that I would like to stress is that the issue of understanding and interpreting of the scope of activities of the security organs is indeed the key issue which is the foundation, the gateway for the entire work and the entire function seen in its entirety. And this issue underlies the -- all the activities of the security organs, and if you don't know this scope, if you don't understand the very concept, it is impossible to understand, evaluate everything that happened and that had to do with the security organs. In this sense, I would just like to say a few important things and -- because there are more but these would just be the most salient ones. The first thing is that the scope defines only the tasks performed by the security organs, and these tasks are later on transformed into the actual assignments. All the other work that is not carried out by security organs are done by other structures within the armed forces or certain civilian elements that are employed by the armed forces. It is especially important to note that because this type of work is labelled "state security" there is a substantial difference and there is a very clear demarcation line between the state security work and other security work that may bear a certain similarity with this work. So this is the first aspect of the scope. The second aspect of the scope of the activities is the part where it is stipulated how security organs actually go about performing these tasks. The third element defines where security organs perform their tasks, the commands, staffs, units, establishments, and organisations for weapons and military equipment in the armed forces. The fourth element regulates the relationship between the security organs and all the other entities involved in performing security tasks, either as organisational units of the armed forces or as individuals, their mutual obligations, mode of communication, and the demarcation of their specific scopes of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained the difference between Article 6 and 7 of the rules of service of the security organs where the security organs are the primary performers of the task and where they are only involved in the performance of the task. Where is the essential difference between those two tasks where the security organ is either an agent or merely participates in the performance of these tasks? That was in paragraphs 11 and 12 of your work.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: When we spoke about the scope of the work, we already noted that there are certain types of work that are clearly delineated from other types of work that belong into the sphere of state security. The purpose of the study that I referred to was to determine whether this demarcation line really exists or obtains in the actual daily work and regular duties of the security organs or whether this line actually becomes blurred and there is an overlap of authority and responsibility in some areas. The security organs at a time when we did this research had to perform quite a lot of tasks that were not part of the state security and that was a significant burden for them and something had to be done to deal with this. And after our research, the tasks were clearly delineated and it was clearly defined what the security organs have to do as agents and what are those tasks where they, as the technical organs of a command, participate in the execution of a task in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've heard quite a few times in the courtroom and you yourself define it here that where the security organs are the agents, that these tasks are called counter-intelligence, and that the tasks where security organs are actually only participants, that these are not counter-intelligence tasks.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The terminology is actually the terminology that is used in practice because in practice, the practice gave us guidance how to define this and this was, in fact, done exactly the way it is. So non-counter-intelligence tasks are tasks where the agents are not security organs but other organs of the command staffs and units and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to page 13 of your expert report, third paragraph in the chapter dealing with the directing of security organs. And here you say: "Other non-counter-intelligence staff security, military police, criminal law tasks where the principal agents or other organs are carried out by security organs in the organisational and establishment units to which they actually are. In this role, as participants in the performance of non-counter-intelligence tasks, the security organs are not doing this as subordinates of their superior security organ."

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Well, this gives you a reflection of the first aspect of the division of tasks. The security organs are participants and other organs are agents, and all the professional tasks, professional direction of the security organs could not be carried out in the usual way because in that way, that superior security organ would be directing the work of another organ which is not subordinate to the security organ. And this is why this was put in place in order to clarify things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You go on to explain about the superior security organs providing professional guidance to the security organs in the subordinate command. Can you please explain to us what does it mean? How is it defined, the provision of technical help, technical assistance, professional guidance and so on? What does it mean? What do the security organs of the superior command do in relation to the security organs of a subordinate command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The professional or technical guidance or provision of assistance and even control in the performance of certain tasks geared towards assisting later, it has to do with the organisation of the work in the performance of these tasks, the application of work methods used in the actual execution of the tasks, the professional capabilities of the subordinate security organ in order to improve them, bring them up to higher level, and to bring them in line with the actual needs. Mutual flow of information to the degree that is necessary to keep the system as a whole functioning. Superior security organs have more information at their disposal. They usually have more experience, and they are better positioned to make proper assessments, and they can thus improve the functioning of the subordinate security organs in terms of their performance of counter-intelligence tasks and in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 13 of your report and page 60 [as interpreted] when you actually describe the facts, the event when the representatives of the security organ of the 1st Military District and of the security administration who arrived in Vukovar on the 19th, this group of officers, are they governed by Article 19, paragraph 3, of the rules of service of the security organs as you just described it to us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: These persons, as I answered before, are persons who have more experience and who are better positioned to actually perform the tasks because they are familiar with the issues they have to deal with when they arrive, and also more aware of the obligations they have to fulfill in relation to the entity that actually dispatched them there. And in this light, it is quite clear that this is not the military chain of command, this is professional and -- this is governed by professionalism or their competence, and they are able to perform this task because they have better capabilities to do so than the unit where the subordinate security organs were supposed to carry out these tasks have. Let me now make a final note. Dispatching such teams is something that is usually decided at a higher level than the level to which they actually belong. And it is quite clear that these are the teams that are actually acting quite independently on the basis of the information and intelligence they get in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is the question that has been discussed at length during the trial, that's the status of the security organs within operational groups and this was studied, this was actually dealt with in paragraph 6 on page 14 in both versions. Here you say that the security organs of the command of the OG direct, in professional terms, the security organs within the units that are now part of the operation group only in the tasks and in the work that is carried out by the security organs, state security, and which serve the functions of providing counter-intelligence security in the performance of the tasks of its unit within the operations group and until the objective has been completed. Can you please explain to us in simple terms what kind of a relationship are we talking about between the two security organs in the operations group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: First of all, we have to bear in mind a few elements if we want to give a proper answer. First of all, operations groups are task forces; they are temporary formations. They are set up in order for the execution of a specific mission, and after that they cease to exist. This means that the operations group command has a temporary mandate to issue orders, to exercise command, and within the organs of the command the security organ is temporarily assigned or appointed to perform tasks to assist in the performance of the overall objective of the operations group. In other words, this means that by carrying out those tasks, the security organ is not treated in the same way. It does not have the same kind of mandate that it would have in a permanent formation. Since it is carrying out these tasks on a temporary basis while the OG is in existence, the security organ is given special task. In principle, this means that the flow of information from the security organ to the security organs in the other units that are part of the OG are quite limited. Let me be more specific. If, in counter-intelligence work, there is no relevant intelligence that should be exchanged between the security organs in the units that are part of the OG and the security organ in the command of the OG, then this function will not actually exist. It will just be the possibility of establishing it until the real need arises. So security organs in the units that are now part of the OG are, in professional terms, subordinate to the security organs in their permanent unit or formation. They submit reports to them and they are accountable to them about counter-intelligence, in general, and any related business. They must take instructions and guidance from them or anything else that a superior security organ is normally responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A brief answer, please. In your work, have you ever encountered anything to indicate that there was a professional link between the security organs of the Guards Brigade and the remain organs that were part of the Operation Group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I have done some research to see whether that link was in fact working. I tried to gather additional information to see if there was any need for a link like that to be functional at all. In both cases, firstly if there were any documents to show that the link indeed functioned, and secondly if there was any need for a link like that to be in place. So in both cases, the answer is I haven't come across anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find any trace or a document in your analysis that there was any link between the security organs of the 1st Military District, on the one hand, and the security organ of OG South on the other?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: There is a problem about this. There is no specific mandate, in a manner of speaking, for the security organ of OG South in terms of the tasks facing them or any provisional authority for them in terms of professional guidance. This of all things was the role of the founder or whoever had established the Operations Group. So there is this vertical line, too, between the Operations Group, on the one hand, and the security organ that had established the Operations Group, but this vertical link didn't work in terms of the exchange of any information about such a function.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can now move on to a set of questions about the relations between the military police and the security organ. Can you tell us, sir, we've heard a lot of references to that, but can you please try to put this in the simplest possible terms as a lecturer. What does it mean when a security organ manages a military police contingent in a professional or technical sense, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In order to have a good answer to this one, it is necessary to point out that the military police and the security organs have different purviews, which means that they use different methods. Likewise, professional guidance in these respective areas requires a certain amount of explanation as to what it means exactly. For a security organ to be in charge of a military police unit, first of all they must be well familiar with the remit of a military police unit. They must know what the situation is that prevails in a given military police unit. They must know what the assignments are that a military police unit faces; and, lastly, they must gather information in order to have the whole picture which would enable them to understand any problems within that military police unit. It is based on all of these factors that they can identify what the best possible use might be for that military police unit and what professional influence might be required for that military police unit to carry out any task received from its superior officer in the best possible way. This is the simplest possible option for a security organ to be in charge of a military police unit. There is a lot more to it, but all of it is a ramification of what you've just told you about how this relationship works globally and what method is applied for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a chart on our screens. The e-court reference is 3D070093. Your Honours, if you go to your binders, this is at tab 10, document number 2. This is a chart of the motorised brigade, attachment 2, it's at the very end of the report in one of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we are waiting for this to come up on our screens, Mr. Vuga, can you please tell us this: What is the distinction between a motorised brigade, especially that belonging to a security organ or the military police, on the one hand, and the Guards Brigade on the other? The English reference is 3D070190. It's part of the report. Mr. Vuga, you have it right there. If you have a textbook motorised brigade, what is it that the security organ does exactly with the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Before I answer that, I must preface my answer with several remarks. The first thing is there is Guards Brigade and there are other types of brigade that were represented in the JNA. There are numerous distinctions between the two. This is by no means the only distinction. This distinction follows from all the other distinctions. It's a matter of purpose for which the Guards Brigade is used and the purpose for which other brigades are used as envisaged in the brigade rules. The infantry, the brigade, the mountain brigade, and all the other brigades. Speaking of this distinction, these distinctions are a direct or indirect result of the first distinction that there is in terms of function. The most fundamental ramification of this would be the following: A Guards Brigade is a very peculiar unit used for specific purposes which are enumerated in my report. You have military police battalions in it, and if you look at the chart, these military police battalions are directly subordinated to the brigade commander. He is the one who hands out tasks to military police commanders, or at least that's what the chart appears to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have it in front of us. The chart about a motorised brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes. I am talking about a military police unit in a brigade like this, as opposed to what I've just been saying. In a motorised brigade, we have a military police unit. This military police unit is subordinated to the brigade commander through the security organ which means that the security organ is a mediator in exercising command over the military police unit and the actual command is then exercised by the brigade commander. But there is a mediator. They are not outside the chain of command. They are a component part, part and parcel of this chain of command. So any orders from the brigade commander to the military police commander are channeled through the security organ, as well as any reports or any other questions between the military police commander and the brigade commander. Again, all of this is channeled through the security commander. Any proposals by the security commander on the use of military police go this way, as well as any decisions on how the military police unit is to be used. It is part and parcel of this working relationship between the brigade commander and the military police commander. One thing that must be noted, however, is that one can never rule out the possibility that based on his own assessment, the commander can issue direct orders to the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that, in fact, the case with the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade is an example that is analogous to this example and there is no major difference in terms of that, simply because the relationships appear to be the same. It -- there may be a difference in terms of methodology but none that I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have attachment number one brought up on our screens. The English is 3D070188, that's the e-court reference, the B/C/S is 3D070091. This is a chart that is part of a book called Guards Brigade Units which has been admitted into evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what this chart is about, sir, and how is this chart different from the other chart that we've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I was talking about this of all things and now we can all see what that means. The military police battalions are at the same level as all the other units directly subordinated to the brigade commander. Between the brigade commander and the battalion -- and the military police battalion commanders, there are no security organs mediating such as is the case with the textbook infantry brigade such as the one shown in the previous chart. This is not a mere formal distinction. We've heard what the security organ does in relation to the military police in an infantry unit, but its role is not shown in the same terms here. But on the other hand, its role is not entirely erased, it's just that the methodology is entirely different. The methodology, however, is not the only difference. The security organ, in relation to the military police, in this type of unit, a unit such as the Guards Brigade, what it should do it can do by making proposals to the brigade commander. Otherwise by trying to exert direct influence upon the military police unit, they would be meddling directly with the chain of command which is neither desirable nor actually allowed. Another thing that must be noted about this chart is the following: The military police battalions, in terms of their actual location, are, to all practical intents, operative units of the brigade and are used for the brigade's functional purpose. The military police in an infantry brigade is normally a unit used for military police-type business within a brigade. There is a certain distinction there, regardless of the fact that in both cases we are looking at military police units. The next thing we see in this chart is the security organ does, after all, have certain tasks that are military police tasks in nature. This is a result of the peculiar nature of the Guards Brigade; that is, a military police corps for special purposes is directly subordinated to the security organ. Its purpose is described specifically in the reports. I won't go any further into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your report, you point out the peculiar nature of the Guards Brigade staff in relation to the military police; Mr. Panic testified to that particular aspect at this trial. Can you tell us what this really means, what is this peculiarity in terms of the Guards Brigade structure and how that structure relates to any military police presence within it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: We see that the security organ does not act as a mediator between the commander and the military police as an organ used for professional guidance of the military police. Because of the peculiar nature of the tasks and use of military police units in the Guards Brigade as well as other units that are at the same level as military police battalions, any units ordered by the commander are elaborated on by the brigade staff and they see to it that these tasks are carried out. In terms of establishment, a brigade has two desk officers specialising in military police business. These officers are required to work on tasks handed out by the commander, tasks that has something to do with the military police. So that the task of the security organ, in terms of being in charge of the military police, for the most part is attached to the brigade staff where you have the desk officers in charge of the military police who have the competence to go about these tasks, who have the qualifications. I have no other information to indicate anything else about the exact structure and how this works.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll now be skipping two whole chapters of your reports, important ones, but I do believe that you will be cross-examined on these. It's about threats to safety in Croatia and the final stages of the Vukovar operation. I'm skipping directly to chapter 5 of your report and the issues addressed therein, which is the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th, 20th and 21st of November. This starts on page 48 or 50 in English. First question, Mr. Vuga, when writing your report, did you come across any document to deal with the regulations that you studied, indicating that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of commanding the hospital evacuation on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I never found a document that would lead me to the unequivocal conclusion that Major Sljivancanin was in command of the evacuation. There is no document to show that anybody at all had been appointed to being commander of the evacuation. No one at all. Not just Major Sljivancanin. So what follows was I was unable to conclude what you suggest. As for the activities that were actually carried out during the evacuation, there is nothing to indicate what the exact command function of any of the people involved was. The only thing one can ascertain is that the nature of the tasks that were carried out, their scope and the performing agents appear in documents under a number of different guises. If you compare these different roles that you come across in the documents, you do get a certain picture as to who did the most in certain ways but without clearly delineated command functions with respect to all of these different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You addressed the issue that I want to raise now on page 50 of your report and the question is this: In light of what we said about the scope of work of the security organs, I want to ask you whether the evacuation of hospital would be within the scope of the activities of the security organs within their purview, in other words, and can a security organ be assigned a task that is outside of its purview and, if so, when, under which circumstances? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: We started from defining the scope of work or the purview of the security organ and we did note that this is something that will keep cropping up. And now I have to refer to the rules -- the part of the rules of service that we have not yet mentioned. The rules of service of the security organ, Article 48, clearly specifies the authority of the commander in issuing tasks to the security organ because the exercise of command is an activity based on law, instructions, and other regulations passed in accordance with the law. So this provision that states that a commander may issue a task to a security organ that are within the purview or the scope of the activities of the security organ that are not carried out at its permanent post, this may lead us to conclude that the commander of the unit may have issued the task to Major Sljivancanin to carry out some security organs that he himself would not be performing in his own brigade but that he may be required to perform within the Operations Group. In other words, these can only be tasks within the purview of the security organ. If we look at the other laws and regulations, even the Federal Secretary of National Defence does not have the power to use the security organs on tasks that are not within their purview. Things are quite different when it comes to military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we will be able to clarify this a little bit later on, and it is, after all, written in your report, this whole issue who assigns tasks to whom. In your report, you did deal with the next issue, but I want to hear it from you. That's pages 56 and 57 in the English version and page 56 in the B/C/S version. You drew certain conclusion on the role played by Colonel Pavkovic in the evacuation of the wounded and the sick on the 20th of November. What do you base your conclusions on and what are the indicators that led you to make these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I inspected the documents, as I already stated in my testimony, that the documents were, in fact, a major source for my conclusions on how the participants, what the participants in this task were actually doing. On the basis of the documents that I had at my disposal, most of them actually indicated that it was Colonel Pavkovic. As for the other participants, there are precious few sources to indicate what they actually were doing. And when you look at the tasks, the nature of these tasks, then you can state that these were very important tasks from the point of view of the person commanding this whole exercise, but one could not really call that person the commander but the actual position would be very close to the position of a commander on the basis of the documents that we studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You saw the testimony of witnesses that we heard during the trial here and to the effect that Major Sljivancanin was in charge of ensuring that there are security conditions in place for the evacuation of the wounded and the sick. So what was Major Sljivancanin, in fact, supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Counsel has made a comment: "You saw the testimony of witnesses that we've heard through the trial that Sljivancanin did as follows." Could he please state who these witnesses are and what he's referring to? Usually when we make a comment, we give a cite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it needs to be specific, Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I think that this is actually in the footnote on pages 57 and 58 but I don't have the paper with the footnotes here in front of me, but this would be testimony by Mr. Sljivancanin, Panic, and Vukasinovic. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic, and see if he accepts that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vuga, as you drafted your report, I showed you the testimony of those witnesses. Do you remember what those witnesses said about the role played or task that Major Sljivancanin had in the evacuation of the hospital, and if you remember that, my question is: What was he supposed to do in light of the rules in the performance of this task? Can you say something about this variation, page 58 of your report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The evaluation of the role played by Mr. Sljivancanin is based on two major sources. The first are the regulations obliging him to put in place the security conditions because as the security organ in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I don't have any footnote referring to that -- any of that testimony. The only footnotes relating to testimony were the footnotes that were related to Panic that were changed from Panic's statements to the Office of the Prosecutor to Panic's testimony. This report was filed in September. These people did not testify in September. We've just had a new version filed on Monday but the contents other than a few changes are pretty much the same. So he could not have drafted his report based on testimony which hadn't even occurred to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's going to be necessary for the Chamber to make any use of this aspect of the report to know what it is based on. If the footnotes don't identify that fully and clearly, you're going to have the witness identify what it was that he relied on. Now, if you're not equipped to do that right now, it may be that that needs to be done in the break. But understand: We need to know what it is the witness has relied on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this, in fact, listed here but these are footnotes 107 and 108; that's transcript -- page of transcript 14294. I think that it is not really necessary, Your Honours, to go into this because the footnotes that are used by the witness are listed here as the reference, and actually there have been some modifications. That may be the cause of the problem, but we can deal with that later but it's not a problem because the Prosecution has it and we provided the references as an attachment to the report that was filed in its entirety and then later on it was modified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just understand, Mr. Lukic, the report is of no value to the Chamber if we don't know what it is based on because we have to evaluate the reliability of what the report was based on. So either now or perhaps more profitably after the break, identify the sources or have the witness do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break, I will hunt down this reference. Apparently I found the wrong footnote here. Perhaps I just misidentified it. Let me now move on to another topic and then I will readdress this issue later on as I near the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, in your report, you explained that the separation of people of military age was the usual expected measure that had to be carried out. But my question to you is: What was the security organ to do once persons who are not supposed to be in the hospital are identified as such?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: First of all, Major Sljivancanin was duty-bound, because of the post that he held, once he was given this task to perform security tasks at the hospital to perform them as his primary task. I don't know whether he was given any other assignments. A security task was the principal task. There are several key issues here that need to be addressed. First of all, a hospital is an institution that has certain standards that have to be complied with throughout an operation, throughout a period in order for it to be considered a protected facility. These standards define the elements that should not be in a hospital and something had to be done in order to identify and remove the elements that do not belong to the hospital because it is impermissible and untenable to take any other measures before this task is done. So the first step to be taken was to deal with the security issues regarding persons who are not supposed to be there. So this is one of the measures that he was duty-bound to take. Secondly, there are combat documents that actually state that the hospital could not be considered as a protected facility during the combat activities for certain reasons, and those reasons are identified. I will not now be quoting my sources, but I can do that. So these are combat documents, not statements. Another thing. There had already been intelligence indicating that there were persons in the hospital whose conduct in the hospital could be labelled a kind of enemy activity against the JNA on the part of the institution that in a way gave them shelter and made it possible for them to perform these kinds of activities, and in such a situation, the security organ has to perform all the tasks as defined by the law, and everything is quite clearly stipulated in the relevant legal provisions, to eliminate such persons and to accord them the appropriate status and to treat them in a way that is stipulated in the Law on Criminal Procedure on the orders of the superior command. So there are at least three foundations for the actions undertaken by Major Sljivancanin in relation to these persons. And it must also be noted that different categories of persons are to be treated differently, and this is something that Major Sljivancanin was supposed to take into account. So this is all based purely on regulations and not -- we are not now going into the intelligence that he may have had at his disposal that indicated to him that the hospital could not have been evacuated until security measures are taken, until the level is reached where the hospital is really nothing more but a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just point out that I found the reference to the testimony by Mr. Panic and Mr. Vukasinovic, that's footnote 113, and here you have the relevant portions of the transcript that I referred to. Just one more topic before the final portion of my examination. The assessment that led to the conclusion that these persons should be transferred to the barracks, is this an adequate, a valid assessment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In my report, I provided the picture of Vukovar from the security point of view. In Vukovar, and this is something that is also stipulated in military regulations, the barracks are facilities that must be the facilities with the highest level of security, provided, of course, that something -- that things that actually happened did not happen. So -- here I'm referring to the blockade of the barracks. But once the barracks was unblocked, once the blockade was lifted, the barracks could be considered as the safest and the most secure place where this activity that had to be carried out should be carried out. And hence the assessment to do this in the barracks, and in fact this assessment is actually the only one that could be made. This was the only place where this could be carried out and this was the only valid conclusion. I couldn't find any other facility that could be used for this purpose in light of the law and intelligence, and once it was stated that the -- that Vukovar was placed under JNA control, from that point onwards, the barracks was, in fact, the safest and the most secure place, much more secure than the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fact that the forward command post was actually situated in the barracks, would that make -- would that corroborate on your conclusion that the barracks was the best place to put those persons, the suspects?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Well, in principle, that would be just an additional element. It's not the decisive factor, but it's one of the things that means that this function must be protected until it is abolished. This only means that any previous activities that had been taken were meant to contribute to the increasing security within -- that prevailed within the barracks itself so that it could be used for its original purpose. So there isn't too much weight that attaches to this, but it certainly affects any evaluation saying that the barracks is a facility that must and can be appropriately used for a purpose like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have five or six minutes left of very specific questions with brief answers expected. If it's a matter of the tape, we can have the break now or else I can press for the remaining five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Press on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, my final questions. Your own assessment, from the point of view of security regulations regarding certain allegations that we have heard throughout this trial, does a unit commander have the power to empower a person not from his unit to give orders to one of the officers in that unit? A brief answer, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: No. Because that person has no power over those persons, and he can only empower the organs of a command to which he is the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who can withdraw an order that has been issued by one of the commanding officers, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Any order issued by a commander can be withdrawn by that same commander or by his superior, at least under the rules of command and control, and the principles enshrined therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What if an officer who previously takes an order from his own commander on withdrawal or, rather, takes it from his superior officer, what he is he required to do at a time like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: If a person receives an order from a superior officer who had previously given him a task, he is required to inform his own commander to indicate that he is no longer able to carry out the tasks that he took from him and that rather now, he will move on and carry out another task which has been given to him by an even higher-ranking officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can a military police officer from one unit take orders from a security organ officer from another unit, any other unit, including the superior command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: We spoke of subordination and the chain of command in terms of military police and command and technical and professional guidance. I would just like to begin something that I said at the outset. Any decision on the use of the military police is made by the commander of the unit within which the military police happens to be, directly or through his subordinate security organ. There is a chain of command that is clearly and unequivocally prescribed and defined. I have not considered any other possibilities outside this chain of command and I don't think there are any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In keeping with that, my next question. A commander of a motorised brigade, if he gives an order to a military police company commander, would the commander of that brigade have the power to withdraw that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: A commander who gives an order in keeping with regulations is free to withdraw any order that he gives as soon as he ascertains that it is no longer justified or that there is no longer any need for it to be carried out. If changes, for example, occur that affect the original nature of his previous order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Much in keeping with what you explained about the security organ of a motorised brigade, can a commander convey this decision through a through his security organ to a military police commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: A commander through his security organ, in terms of establishment, I mean, can hand out orders to the military police, whatever orders he may deem necessary. He receives professional guidance from the security organ for this purpose. A typical example would be in a brigade such as the 80th Brigade because -- I apologise, I must point out one thing, lest it be forgotten. Because the security organ is a mediator between the military police and the commander, in professional terms or technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I would now like to tender Mr. Vuga's report into evidence. I think we will just give up the annexes purely for ease of handling or to avoid any difficulties. So we want the expert report and the attachments in evidence. As for the remaining 65 ter documents, I thought that was best left for the end of this witness's appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we'll deal with it on our return at five minutes to 3.00 when you will indicate the nature of the sources relied on if you have them identified in footnotes or, failing that, have the witness specify the sources relied on for his report. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first I would like to provide a clarification to avoid any misunderstanding about what I said previously. Mr. Vuga's report contains an annex and three attachments -- or, rather, four attachments. When we proofed Mr. Vuga, we proofed him in keeping with your instructions. The same method as was applied with Mr. Pringle, which is what Mr. Moore requested about a week ago. Previously, when Mr. Vuga had drafted his first report in July, he had been using statements made by certain persons as his sources. We now showed him various transcripts of those same persons' evidence and these are now invoked in his footnotes, in the footnotes of his present report. He no longer invokes any statements but rather the evidence given by those witnesses. If you remember what Mr. Moore highlighted in different colours with Mr. Pringle the parts of statements that weren't relevant and were therefore not made evidence. All the footnotes that you have in the final version of the report indicate Mr. Vuga's reliance on evidence. So these are the amendments that were made to the footnotes. I think there is one particular reference to a person's statement. We didn't manage to track that one down in any of the transcripts and we just edited that out of the report. We have been in touch with Mr. Weiner over the last several days and we have kept him informed in a timely manner about everything. So what I am now tendering into evidence is Mr. Vuga's report with the four attachments, but no annex. As for the evidence he invokes for rather the exhibits from the 65 ter list, in order not to waste more time with Mr. Vuga, I thought the same procedure might be applied as with Mr. Theunens, previously. Once our Defence case is over, we would like to individually tender these documents into evidence or have them marked for identification as well as a number of other documents that we shall be tendering under Rule 92 bis afterwards. I think this would be the most meaningful way to go about this and not use Mr. Vuga's presence in the courtroom for each and every one of these documents. That was the clarification that I was hoping to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as we understand it, you say that with the corrections that have been made, the corrigenda, the report in the footnotes indicates all the documents relied on by the witness. Thank you, I see your nod in concurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing that would like to explain is the amended version is part of our e-court system. There is an electronic copy which was inserted today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Weiner, the objection, is it maintained as the annex is not now being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There's no objection with the annex being removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The report with the attachments but no annex will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 868, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, thank you, Mr. Lukic, for all of that and for the timely handling of things. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vuga.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am Vladimir Domazet. I will be asking you questions on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's Defence team. I'll start with the evacuation. I will pick up where you left off in answer to one of my learned friend's Mr. Lukic's questions, page 76, selecting the barracks of all places as the most appropriate facility. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What exactly did you establish? Who decided that prisoners should be taken to the barracks and when?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is about the fact that the barracks was the most appropriate facility for this purpose. The barracks was an installation in Vukovar that was the most appropriate one for prisoners to be taken to in order to make sure that they were safe, at least -- with all the relevant standards in place. But I don't have anything to equivocally indicate who decided that the prisoners would be sent to the barracks. I did not find any paper trail. There are statements made at briefings and other meetings but I didn't take that to be the final position. There is nothing in writing to indicate that a final decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why did you not take that to be the final position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I could only have done that if I had taken into account the statement made by the Chief of Staff, but that wasn't the option that I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you suggesting -- Mr. Panic is probably the person you have in mind, right? Are you suggesting that Mr. Panic had said that the barracks had been selected as the place to which the prisoners would be taken?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Based on my memory, there was talk of the barracks at that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But for the Chamber, the transcript reference is 14295. Mr. Panic is on record as saying that the barracks was never mentioned. They were supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica and the convoy was supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica, so he didn't mention it. You might have had someone else in mind. When you say the choice of the barracks is the most appropriate place under the assumption that there was a check-point at the gate, somebody checking at the gate, that it was secured according to the regulations and that it met all the requirements for any barracks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: There are clear-cut regulations governing how a barracks is organised and set up. There is no proviso for the fact that a barracks might not meet all these requirements or, in other words, not really be sufficiently safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you because of what various witnesses have suggested as well as the fact that many people who just didn't belong there happened to be inside the barracks at the same time that the buses were there. The explanation preferred by the witnesses was they were coming in in all sorts of ways, the fence was not complete, there were holes in the fence and people just kept coming in. How, then, would you still maintain that the barracks as such was a safe place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: A barracks is not guarded by a fence; it is guarded by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fair enough. You say the barracks was selected as a holding centre.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I studied documents about the barracks, and I also relied on my experience as someone who lived and worked in a barracks. So when I studied the situation in Vukovar, I concluded that this was the most appropriate place because of the elements that I've addressed. Were all the elements in place, well, it was up to whoever was in charge of the barracks, whoever was the barracks commander to make sure that they were and to what degree exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you studied this from a theoretical point of view when you made your report? You didn't study the actual situation that prevailed in Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I did study the situation as it was, but I also had to take into account the very definition of a barracks in all the rules and regulations governing work in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Looking at the various documents of this case, did you ever realise that both Velepromet and Ovcara had also been used as holding centres or collection points?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I found all the various procedures in relation to Velepromet. But it wasn't defined just as a collection point, it was defined as a place where a triage was conducted of persons who, after the end of operations, were still not taken care of and still did not know where they would go next or where their future lay. It was from there that persons were selected who were to be treated as prisoners of war. In relation to a number of such persons, as far as I was able to ascertain based on documents, the barracks was, in fact, taken into consideration for a while, but they didn't stay there for too long. I realise that the Mitnica group that surrendered had laid down their arms and had been put up at the Ovcara facility. On the 18th and on the 19th, they were taken to Sremska Mitrovica and all the standards were applied that applied to prisoners of war, those who had laid down their arms and had put up no resistance, everything that applied under the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you studied this, did you perhaps come across anything to indicate that Ovcara was one of the places designated as a POW camp?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The fact that Ovcara was designated as a POW camp was the indication concerning where the Mitnica group would be put up, so that's all that I came across. Rather, when the actual location was selected; that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your position is that the hospital evacuation was not a job for a security organ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that, do you mean the evacuation of the actual patients or the evacuation that was supposed to take place that obviously was not meant to include just the patients or any civilians found in the hospital, but also was meant to include crime suspects?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: At this point and earlier on when I thought about this, I bore in mind the evacuation as a unified task. If you look at the position of the Croatian side, they had by no means done everything within their power to comply with all the regulations regarding the hospital. They knew there would be an evacuation and they did all within their power to create circumstances that were impossible. I firmly believe that the situation as it was at the hospital required all the steps that were taken from the security aspect. Also, you must say that their hand was forced in the way by the Croatian side. It was something foisted on them by the Croats. This was meant to be an evacuation, a unified task with the usual procedure as it was eventually carried out, but at the outset it was certainly a single task, and that's what I mean when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If you don't think this is a job for a security organ, who is it a job for then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is something for the unit commander to decide. I was in no position myself to reflect on that, of who that might have been. One needed to know the situation and the openings at the time, and the openings were limited. If anyone, it should have been a different officer in different position. Under the existing regulations, this was most certainly not a job for any security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your report, you invoked statements made by witnesses. Most of the times you invoked the statements of Colonel Panic, right? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I invoked Lieutenant-Colonel Panic to the degree that he was involved and to the degree that these things happened through him without the active participation of other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were you aware of the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic at page 14294 had said before this Trial Chamber that Sljivancanin had been given an assignment for the 20th of November, the morning of the 20th of November to proceed with the hospital evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember that part of Panic's evidence and I can't, not because I don't want to but because I -- it may have slipped my mind. I would have to read it and then view it in the context and then assess the actual value of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was mentioned at the next page, 14295 was shown to you, and does that mean that the previous page 14294 was not shown to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I simply said that I couldn't remember this part of his testimony. If what you say is true, if he in fact really did state that, then I would have to view this statement in the context of the overall evidence and then tell you what it means. I can't do it like this, out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now let us go to page 49 of the B/C/S version, and let us go to paragraph B1, I hope that the English speakers will be able to find it, where it says that Colonel -- that Major Sljivancanin was also appointed among other officers by Colonel Mile Mrksic. Were you able to identify the other officers that you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The term that is mentioned here actually referred to the medical staff, the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So when you said "other officers," you meant medical staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, I meant the doctors, because they are also military officers at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you analysed all the documents, did you learn or did you perhaps learn from some other sources about a telegram that was sent by General Aco Vasiljevic. I don't know if you know what I mean. Do you have any comments about that, or do I have to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I did not see the text of the telegram, so any comments I might make would be inappropriate because I would not know the actual contents of the telegram. I could do so on the basis of what I heard about the telegram and its contents, but that would be inappropriate and insufficient for any conclusions to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to state for the record I have just checked pages 14294 and 14295 of Colonel Panic's testimony and the words that my learned colleague just quoted as having been uttered by Mr. Panic are not there regarding Mr. Sljivancanin being put in charge of the evacuation of the hospital. I simply could not find any such reference in the two pages of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't check it now, but I'm quite sure 14294, on that page of the transcript, this is Panic's evidence of the 8th of November where he discusses the appointment or the task that Major Sljivancanin was given on the 20th in the morning, and the next page, 95, there he talks about how the convoy was supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica and no mention is made of neither the barracks or Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, are you aware of what Mr. Panic said at page 14318 of the transcript, that he was surprised when he saw the buses at the barracks because this had not been planned and he should have known -- he should have been aware of it had any such orders been issued? Some other witnesses mentioned this fact too.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I cannot make any comments as to whether he was or was not surprised, because the fact that he was surprised would not tell me how he was surprised at seeing the buses at the barracks because there are no other comments as to why he was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. He says because this had not been envisaged or planned. Does it mean that this was not envisaged in the task?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: There is a number of other options, other elements that have to be taken into account by an expert to be able to draw any conclusions. Please do not make me speculate. He should have specified why he was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you were unable to conclude who had issued the order for the buses to go to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I was unable to draw any unequivocal conclusions so I could not really maintain that such and such a person had issued the order for the buses to go to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During the proofing sessions, were you told who had testified to this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was Ljubisa Vukasinovic. This is as far as I'm able to remember, so this is the caveat I have to put in place here, because in my view this was not a crucial element for the choice. This was obviously what it was. These prisoners were obviously taken to Sremska Mitrovica in stages, and this is something that is stipulated in the rules of service of the military police and the instruction of the implementation of the rules of service of military police, so this was not -- this would not be in contravention of the existing regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you now go to page 62 of your report. I'm interested in paragraph 7(3).

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this is item 2. I will read it out to you and then you can tell us what you think of it. So this is 7(3) --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We can't seem to find the page but there's a method actually to finding pages quickly. If counsel can just state a footnote number that's on the page, then we can usually find things much quicker. So if you say page 59 in the B/C/S but there's a footnote 58 on there, we can then try and find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner, that may be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The footnote is 124 on this page where we have paragraph 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me read: "Major Sljivancanin, on the basis of existing regulations and the criteria for the barracks as a military facility, could conclude that the prisoners of war, after their safe conduct from the hospital to the barracks and the disposition of the buses, with the direct security in place in the barracks compound that they would have -- enjoy full security including the security necessary for their transfer to Sremska Mitrovica." Is this stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you explain, does it mean that it was your view that Major Sljivancanin decided this or what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is what it says here verbatim. He could realistically conclude, in light of the nature of the barracks as the military facility, that it could be used to put the prisoners of war there. So he could make a realistic conclusion to that effect in light of the existing regulations and the criteria that applied to the barracks as a military facility. This is all that it says here, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. There were some objections regarding Mr. Panic's evidence. My colleague, Mr. Vasic, was able to locate the reference about the evacuation. So this -- the reference can be found at page 14384 and 14385. While we are on this page of your report, paragraph 7(4), you quote an entry from the war log; the date is the 20th of November. Does it say here that the activity regarding the cleaning, evacuation and the transport of the civilian population from Ovcara, Velepromet and the Vukovar Hospital. That's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that the civilian population is the only category listed here and no other?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a little while ago that as regards the buses, you -- that people should have gathered some place. You probably had in mind the witness testimony to the effect that first the three buses left and then the two buses after them. Are you aware that the witnesses, in particular those who were on the buses, that they testified that all the buses left at the same time from the hospital to the barracks, and from the barracks to the -- to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the manner in which the buses moved, if we looked at it from the security point of view, is quite irrelevant, both in terms of the security measures and the place of accommodation. The only relevant point here, as regards the buses, is that when people boarded the buses in the barracks, they should not have remained there for a long time. And now, how long is long or short it's something that one needs to assess. This is the only relevant element when it comes to the transport. Now whether the buses moved three by three or all six at the same time, it didn't matter because there were no security risks en route from the hospital to the barracks, and these are the facts relevant for the security -- for the transport on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you able to determine who actually had decided for the buses to go to Ovcara at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: From the elements that I have been shown so far, it is impossible to identify the person who actually decided that the prisoners of war should go to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, in light of your answer to my penultimate question when you said that it could have been done in this way or any other way, was it proper to organise a convoy in such a way that there is a special vehicle marked in a proper way at the beginning of the -- at the head of the column and at the rear of the column or convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: What convoy do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
